title: 12 — Graphs and Knowledge Graphs
html:
12 — Graphs and Knowledge Graphs

The one idea: many financial questions are about connections, not rows: who owns whom, who lends to whom, which records are the same company. A graph stores those connections directly. Every edge should carry dates and evidence, so you can ask what the network looked like on any day.

1. What it is

Term Meaning
Graph Nodes (entities) and edges (relationships)
Property graph Nodes and edges carry key-value properties. Used by GraphFrames, NetworkX, Neo4j and others
RDF graph Facts as subject, predicate, object triples, with web identifiers (IRIs). The model behind ontologies such as FIBO, queried with SPARQL
Knowledge graph A graph of entities, documents, definitions and relationships, often with an ontology on top, used as context for products and agents
GraphFrames Graph processing on Spark DataFrames: a vertex DataFrame (id) and an edge DataFrame (src, dst)
NetworkX Python library for graph analysis in memory on one machine

2. Why it matters

  • Entity resolution is a graph problem: matched records form clusters, and each cluster is one entity.
  • Early-warning and contagion signals come from paths: a promoter pledge, a group company, a common lender.
  • Agents answer better with context: a graph lets them walk relationships and cite the path.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Property graph or RDF?

Property graph RDF
Strength Fast traversal and algorithms, easy to build from tables Shared meaning, standard vocabularies (FIBO), reasoning
Query Graph APIs, Cypher-like languages SPARQL
Fit here Relationship analytics, entity clusters Ontology and class definitions, interchange

A common pattern is to keep the ontology in RDF (what a LegalEntity is) and the instance relationships as property-graph edge tables in the lakehouse (who owns whom, with dates).

3.2 Algorithms you will use

Algorithm Question
Connected components (union-find) Which records belong to the same entity?
Breadth-first search, shortest path How is A connected to B?
PageRank and centrality Which entities are most central to the network?
Community detection Which groups of entities cluster together?
Motif finding (GraphFrames) Find patterns such as A→B→C→A

3.3 Dated edges

---
title: Dated relationship graph — the path exists only on some dates
---
flowchart LR
    AH["Alpha Holdings"] -- "owns 51%<br/>2019-04-01 to open" --> AF["Alpha Finance"]
    AF -- "lends to<br/>2024-06-01 to 2026-03-31" --> BI["Beta Infra"]
    BI -- "guaranteed by<br/>2025-01-15 to open" --> GP["Gamma Power"]
    AH -- "owns 26%<br/>2021-07-01 to 2025-12-31" --> DR["Delta Realty"]

Store edges as a table with src, dst, relation, valid_from, valid_to, evidence_id. Filter by date before building the graph, and the same algorithm then answers "as of" questions.

3.4 Scale

  • NetworkX: in memory, one machine. Good up to millions of edges, depending on the algorithm.
  • GraphFrames: on Spark, for bigger graphs and batch jobs. Spark Connect artifacts appeared on Maven Central in 2026 (0.11.0 in March, 0.12.x in June). The Python package needs the JVM part installed on the cluster.
  • A dedicated graph database is worth adding only when a product needs interactive traversal at low latency.

4. Working code

The script clusters six made-up source records into entities with union-find, then finds a path between two companies over dated edges on two dates. Standard library only.

from collections import deque

# 1. Entity resolution as a graph problem: records are nodes, accepted matches are edges,
#    and each connected component is one real-world entity. Union-find computes components fast.
records = ["R1:exchange", "R2:registry", "R3:annual-report", "R4:vendor", "R5:news", "R6:vendor"]
matches = [("R1:exchange", "R2:registry", "same CIN"),
           ("R2:registry", "R3:annual-report", "same CIN"),
           ("R4:vendor", "R1:exchange", "same ISIN of issued bond"),
           ("R5:news", "R6:vendor", "name + city, p=0.94")]
parent = {r: r for r in records}
def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]        # path halving keeps trees flat
        x = parent[x]
    return x
for a, b, _ in matches:
    parent[find(a)] = find(b)
clusters = {}
for r in records:
    clusters.setdefault(find(r), []).append(r)
for i, members in enumerate(sorted(clusters.values()), start=1):
    print(f"ENT-{i:03d}: {members}")

# 2. A dated relationship graph: edges are valid only between two dates.
edges = [  # (from, relation, to, valid_from, valid_to)
    ("Alpha Holdings", "owns_51pct", "Alpha Finance", "2019-04-01", None),
    ("Alpha Finance", "lends_to", "Beta Infra", "2024-06-01", "2026-03-31"),
    ("Beta Infra", "guaranteed_by", "Gamma Power", "2025-01-15", None),
    ("Alpha Holdings", "owns_26pct", "Delta Realty", "2021-07-01", "2025-12-31"),
]
def neighbours(node, as_of):
    for f, rel, t, vf, vt in edges:
        if vf <= as_of and (vt is None or as_of <= vt):
            if f == node: yield rel, t
            if t == node: yield f"inverse({rel})", f

def path(src, dst, as_of):
    seen, q = {src}, deque([(src, [src])])
    while q:
        node, p = q.popleft()
        if node == dst:
            return p
        for rel, nxt in neighbours(node, as_of):
            if nxt not in seen:
                seen.add(nxt)
                q.append((nxt, p + [f"-{rel}->", nxt]))
    return None

for as_of in ("2025-06-30", "2026-10-26"):
    print(f"As of {as_of}: Alpha Holdings to Gamma Power ->", path("Alpha Holdings", "Gamma Power", as_of))

Output:

ENT-001: ['R1:exchange', 'R2:registry', 'R3:annual-report', 'R4:vendor']
ENT-002: ['R5:news', 'R6:vendor']
As of 2025-06-30: Alpha Holdings to Gamma Power -> ['Alpha Holdings', '-owns_51pct->', 'Alpha Finance', '-lends_to->', 'Beta Infra', '-guaranteed_by->', 'Gamma Power']
As of 2026-10-26: Alpha Holdings to Gamma Power -> None

What to notice:

  • Four records chain into one entity, through two CIN matches and one ISIN link, even though R4 and R3 never matched each other directly. That is what connected components add over pairwise matching.
  • On 2025-06-30 there is a three-hop path from Alpha Holdings to Gamma Power. On 2026-10-26 there is none, because the loan ended on 2026-03-31. Same algorithm, different date.

The GraphFrames equivalent, not run here (it needs Spark with the GraphFrames package):

# Not run.
from graphframes import GraphFrame
v = spark.table("silver.entities").select("id", "name")
e = (spark.table("silver.relationships")
       .where("valid_from <= '2025-06-30' AND (valid_to IS NULL OR valid_to >= '2025-06-30')")
       .select("src", "dst", "relation"))
g = GraphFrame(v, e)
spark.sparkContext.setCheckpointDir("/Volumes/fin/tmp/checkpoints")   # required by connectedComponents
clusters = g.connectedComponents()
paths = g.bfs("name = 'Alpha Holdings'", "name = 'Gamma Power'", maxPathLength=4)

5. Common mistakes

  1. Edges without dates. You can't answer "as of", and old links pollute today's signals.
  2. Edges without evidence. An analyst can't check why two companies are linked.
  3. Pairwise matching without clustering. A matches B and B matches C, but A and C stay apart. Use connected components.
  4. Over-merging through one bad edge. A single wrong match can join two large clusters. Review bridge edges and big merges.
  5. A graph database first. Start with edge tables and batch algorithms. Add a graph store when a product needs it.

6. Exercise (1.5 hours)

  1. Add a deliberately wrong match edge that joins the two clusters, then write a check that flags any merge creating a cluster of more than five records.
  2. Add a pledge_pct property to ownership edges, and find all companies whose promoter has pledged more than 50% as of a date.
  3. Rebuild the same graph in NetworkX and run nx.pagerank.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why is entity resolution a connected-components problem?
  2. When would you use RDF rather than a property graph?
  3. How do you ask a graph "as of" a date?
  4. What does GraphFrames need on the cluster besides the Python package?
  5. What is the risk of a single bad match edge?

Answers

  1. Matches are edges, and transitive chains (A–B, B–C) must collapse into one entity, which is exactly a connected component.
  2. For shared definitions, standard vocabularies such as FIBO, reasoning and interchange.
  3. Store valid-from and valid-to on every edge, and filter edges to the date before running the algorithm.
  4. The JVM library, on the cluster or the Spark Connect server.
  5. It can merge two large, unrelated clusters into one wrong entity.
